summary: A reprinted magazine article by two industry writers discussing how to define the Internet and how big it is, since estimates varied widely in the press. It is informational and not a specification.

eli5.summary: People argued about how big the Internet was, depending on how they counted. This article looks at what should count and why it is hard to say.

questions: is fido net part of the internet
what is the difference between the core internet and consumer internet
subtitle: Defining the Internet by its interactive services and boundaries

tldr.problem: In the mid-1990s, the press, marketers, and the public used the term 'Internet' very loosely, claiming sizes ranging from thousands to millions based on different definitions, causing confusion about what the Internet actually was.
tldr.mechanism: This article proposes defining the Internet by its core characteristic: networks using IP that support interactive services like WWW, FTP, TELNET, and email, distinguished from asynchronous-only systems like UUCP and FidoNet.
tldr.outcome: The authors introduce a framework of concentric categories: the core Internet (suppliers and consumers), the consumer Internet (consumers only), and the Matrix (mail-only systems), making it possible to measure and discuss different network tiers meaningfully.

today: RFC 1935 is an Informational article and reflects the Internet's state in 1994-1996, when interactive services like the WWW were new. The definitions and concerns about network boundaries remain conceptually relevant, though the prevalence of always-on broadband, mobile IP, and public cloud services have blurred some of the categories the authors described.

sections.title: The Confusion Over Size
sections.content:
The authors note that newspapers, marketers, and industry observers claimed widely different sizes for the Internet in 1994, with some saying it is larger than others claim. The dispute arose from a New York Times article quoting one of the RFC authors, which sparked debate over whether the Internet was actually smaller than other estimates suggested.

The real issue beneath the size debate is a more fundamental question: what should count as the Internet at all? People were including computers that were not yet connected, or might connect in the future. The authors prefer to count only systems actually connected now, and define what services qualify a network as part of the Internet.
sections.eli5: Different people counted different things as the Internet, so they got different sizes. This article says you should only count things actually hooked up right now, not things that might connect later.

sections.title: Interactive Services Distinguish the Internet
sections.content:
The RFC argues that the distinguishing feature of the Internet is interactive services: WWW, Gopher, FTP, and TELNET. These protocols allow a user to request something and get a response in real time. By contrast, email, USENET news, and UUCP are asynchronous, batch, and store-and-forward services where messages are queued for later delivery, not delivered interactively.

The authors note that networks like FidoNet and UUCP can carry email and news but do not support interactive services. Therefore, they argue, these networks should not be called part of the Internet, even though they exchange mail. The defining service of the Internet is not email (which has existed since 1972) but the interactive services that caught the public's imagination.

One key principle: interactive vs. asynchronous is different from direct vs. dialup. A dialup IP connection can support all interactive services equally well; the type of connection is less important than the presence of IP and interactive capabilities.
sections.eli5: The Internet is when you ask a computer something and get an answer right away. Email and news are when you send something and wait for an answer later. That is the big difference.

sections.title: Core, Consumer, and Matrix
sections.content:
The authors propose three concentric categories. The core Internet consists of networks and hosts that can both receive and send interactive services (supplier-capable). The consumer Internet adds computers behind firewalls that can receive interactive services but may not easily host them (consumer-capable). The Matrix encompasses all systems worldwide that exchange email, including the Internet, UUCP networks, FidoNet, and commercial mail systems.

A firewalled enterprise network, for example, is part of the consumer Internet if it can reach WWW and FTP servers outside the firewall. A company may keep one or two servers at the firewall boundary to serve its own users, but its clients cannot easily serve resources back out.

Email, USENET news, and mail lists mostly pass through firewalls in both directions because they are asynchronous and less of a security risk. This distinction between what interactive and asynchronous services can do is key to understanding why firewalls distinguish supplier-capable from consumer-capable networks.
sections.eli5: The Internet has layers like a Russian doll. The inner core is computers that can both ask for and offer services. Around it is consumers who can ask for services but cannot easily offer them. Around that is everyone who can use email.

sections.title: IP as the Internet's Foundation
sections.content:
The authors define the Internet as requiring IP (Internet Protocol) to permit users to use interactive services. Some objected that this was too technical or too restrictive, and that other protocol suites with application gateways could provide the same services. The authors respond that IP was not chosen arbitrarily: there is something about IP and the Internet ecosystem that is especially conducive to the development of new interactive protocols.

They also note the concept of different degrees of IP to the user. A shell login on a provider's system gives text-only interactive access; IP to the user's own computer with a graphical display enables the full graphical experience of protocols like WWW and Mosaic. Both qualify as Internet access, but the degree of capability is different.
sections.eli5: The Internet uses IP because IP was what made interactive services possible. Without IP, you cannot have the interactive features that make the Internet the Internet.

sections.title: Networks In and Out of the Framework
sections.content:
Commercial conferencing systems like Prodigy and CompuServe support email and news but not the characteristic interactive services. CompuServe users understand that they use 'Internet mail' (email sent to the Internet) but do not regard CompuServe itself as the Internet. Similarly, commercial mail networks like MCI Mail and Sprint-Mail are part of the Matrix but not the Internet.

Large isolated networks outside the framework exist too: France's Minitel (Teletel), company LANs using AppleTalk or Novell NetWare that are not connected to anything else, and private mainframe systems. These fall outside all categories because they exchange no services with other networks.

The article also notes that people have historically tried to equate the Internet with other networks: the ARPANET in the 1970s-80s, NSFNET in the late 1980s, and USENET in the early 1990s. Each time, the equation was wrong. The Internet is simply the Internet, with its own definition.
sections.eli5: CompuServe has email to the Internet, but it is not part of the Internet. Big private networks inside companies do not count because they do not talk to anything outside.
